product.title: Pashto 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Pashto: the Pashto-Arabic script with a pronunciation guide under every line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Pashto builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of all 44 letters with their joined forms, the eight letters found in neither Arabic nor Persian, numbers 1–100, an A1 grammar summary, and the fifty most common verbs. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from prepositions that come in pairs and wrap around their noun to past-tense sentences whose verb agrees with the object, not the subject.

blocks.text: Pashto is rarely taught anywhere. Look for a course and you will struggle to find one; look for a good self-study book and the shelf is nearly empty. Yet it is the mother tongue of some forty million people, one of the two official languages of Afghanistan, and the everyday language of all of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan. This course was written to fill that gap — and it assumes you are starting from absolute zero.

What is not zero is what you bring. The alphabet is the Arabic script, and if you have met it before, your eyes already have a head start. The vocabulary is full of words that also live in Arabic, Persian, Urdu, and Hindi — *kitāb* (book), *wakht* (time), *dunyā* (world), *khabar* (news), *bāzār*, *sābūn* (soap) — and a handful that are cousins of English words. And the numbers, after twenty, are far tidier than French or Danish ones.

But don't be fooled by the script. **Pashto is not Arabic.** It is an Indo-European language, a distant cousin of Persian, and further back a cousin of Sanskrit, Greek, and English. There are no verb patterns (wazn), no case endings (i'rab), no article *al-*. Instead there are two things Arabic does not have: **nouns with a gender that spreads to their adjectives and verbs**, and **past-tense sentences that turn the whole structure around**.

Those two things are what make people give up in the second month — not the script, not the vocabulary. This course introduces both slowly and earlier than most books do: gender arrives in unit 2 and comes back in every unit after it; the inverted past sentence is introduced in unit 13, with a full unit of its own, after twelve units have prepared the ground.

blocks.title: Three gifts and three traps
items: **Gift 1 — "to have" is an ordinary verb.** Persian, Urdu, Arabic, and Hebrew all go the long way round to say "I have". Pashto does not: زه یو کتاب لرم = "I one book have". Just like English, except that the verb goes at the end.
**Gift 2 — no articles.** No *the*, no *a*, no *al-*. کتاب can mean "book", "a book", or "the book", depending on context.

**Gift 3 — part of the vocabulary may already be yours.** Through Arabic and Persian, hundreds of everyday Pashto words are shared with Urdu, Hindi, Persian, and Turkish — and a few with English. A page further on lists them.
**Trap 1 — nouns have gender, and it spreads.** کتاب is masculine, ښځه feminine; adjectives, demonstratives, and verbs change to match. English has nothing quite like it.
**Trap 2 — prepositions come in pairs and wrap around the noun.** "In Kabul" is not په کابل but **په** کابل **کې** — one word before, one after. Unit 6 is devoted to this.
**Trap 3 — in the past tense, the verb agrees with the OBJECT.** "I read the book" becomes ما کتاب ولوست, and the form ولوست is decided by **کتاب**, not by "I". Unit 13 does nothing else.

blocks.text: One more thing to get straight from the start. You may have learned to read Arabic letters for the Qur'an or for another language, and that practice is valuable — your eyes already recognize the shapes. But Pashto asks for something else: recognizing **eight letters that exist in neither Arabic nor Persian** (ټ ډ ړ ڼ ږ ښ ځ څ), and training your tongue for sounds made with its tip curled back. Two pages further on deal with all of this in one go, and after that the letters will not trip you up again.

The twenty units ahead are built in layers: each one reuses what the previous ones put in place, and each one targets exactly one of the spots that most often trip up learners. Work through them in order, one unit per sitting, twenty to thirty minutes. By the end of unit 20 you will be able to introduce yourself, bargain in a Kabul bazaar, make plans for tomorrow, talk about yesterday, and write short messages that sound like someone from Jalalabad — not like a translation.

blocks.text: The ground rules that make this course work

items: **One unit per sitting.** Twenty to thirty minutes. Never two units at once — what sticks is not what is plentiful but what is repeated the next day.
**Read aloud.** Pashto has sounds English does not, and your eyes cannot train your tongue. If you feel shy, whispering is fine — what matters is that your mouth moves.
**Don't memorize the tables.** The tables are for looking things up, not for learning by heart. What sticks is whole sentences from the dialogues.
**Reread yesterday's dialogue before starting a new unit.** Five minutes. This is the one habit that really decides the result.
**Write by hand.** Pashto script is joined, and the hand remembers the joined shapes much faster than the eye.

blocks.title: About the pronunciation guide in this course
items: The pronunciation is written in Latin letters under every Pashto line. It is a **temporary aid** — as soon as you can read the script yourself, cover that column.

Long vowels carry a bar on top: **ā ī ū**. No bar means short. The letter **ə** is the short *a* in *about* — short, unrounded, and extremely common in Pashto. **e** is like the *e* in *café*, **o** like the *o* in *go* (without the *w* glide), **ay** like *y* in *my*, and **aw** like *ow* in *how*.
Letters with a dot underneath — **ṭ ḍ ṛ ṇ** — are said with the tip of the tongue **curled back** to touch the roof of the mouth. English does not have these sounds, and the next page trains them.
**ṣ** and **ẓ** are two typically Pashto letters (ښ and ږ) whose sound **differs by region**. The next page explains; for now, just know that neither is a misprint.

The mark **'** stands for the letter ع, which in Afghanistan is nearly always pronounced very lightly or not at all. **kh** is the *ch* of Scottish *loch*, **gh** a soft gargled *r* like French *r*, and **q** a *k* made deep in the throat.

front.title: Hundreds of Pashto words you may already know

blocks.text: Pashto has borrowed thousands of words from Arabic and Persian — the same words that also live in Urdu, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, and Indonesian, and some that reached English. If you know any of those languages, you start with a vocabulary already in place. The table below is only a sample; once your ear is tuned, you will catch these words yourself in the middle of a sentence.
Seven borrowed words whose meaning shifted on the way

Borrowing is never neat. Some of these words also travelled to Malay and Indonesian, where they took on a different meaning — so if you know those languages (or meet a speaker), these are the words that cause confident misunderstandings.

blocks.title: And what Arabic does not have: native Pashto words
items: The backbone of the language is not Arabic at all. The words you use most every day — ور (door), لار (road), سترګه (eye), لاس (hand), اوبه (water), ډوډۍ (bread/food), کور (house), ښځه (woman), سړی (man) — are all native Pashto, not borrowings.

Some of them are even distant relatives of English through their Indo-European roots: مور (*mor*) and *mother*, پلار (*plār*) and *father*, ورور (*wror*) and *brother*, نوم (*nūm*) and *name*, درې (*dre*) and *three*.

That likeness is neither chance nor borrowing — Pashto and English grew from the same ancient parent language. If you ever thought the language of Afghanistan must be "another kind of Arabic", here is the proof that it isn't.

front.title: Pashto script: 44 letters, eight of them new

blocks.text: The Pashto script is the Arabic script extended twice: once by Persian (پ چ ژ ګ), and once more by Pashto itself (ټ ډ ړ ڼ ږ ښ ځ څ). If you can already read Arabic letters, two-thirds of the way is covered. This page takes care of the rest.
Eight letters that exist in neither Arabic nor Persian

*n* with the tongue curled back. Never at the start of a word.
In Kandahar: *sh* with the tongue curled back. In Kabul & Jalalabad: like **kh**.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Two letters, two regions: ښ and ږ — and why this course does not choose
items: Pashto has two major dialects. In the **south** (Kandahar, Helmand, Quetta) ښ is a curled-back *sh* and ږ a curled-back *zh*. In the **east and north** (Kabul, Jalalabad, Peshawar) ښ sounds exactly like **kh** and ږ exactly like **g**.
So ښه ("good") sounds like *ṣa* in Kandahar and *kha* in Kabul. Both are correct, both are understood everywhere, and nobody will laugh at you.

This course writes **ṣ** and **ẓ** in the pronunciation column so that each letter still matches its script one to one — if it were written *kh*, you would never know which is ښ and which is خ when you write.

**My advice: choose the Kabul pronunciation** (ښ = *kh*, ږ = *g*) if you are aiming for central and northern Afghanistan — it is the pronunciation of Kabul television. Choose Kandahar if you are learning for the south. What matters: **choose one and don't switch back and forth.**

Vowels, and the typically Pashto word endings

rows: long *a*, as in *father*. At the start of a word written آ or ا.
Three jobs at once, depending on the word.
long *e*, as in *café*. **Not found in Arabic or Persian.**
Ending of **feminine** nouns: ډوډۍ *ḍoḍəy* (bread). Always at the end of a word.
Verb ending for "you (pl.)": ښه یاست؟ · راځئ *rādzəy* (come on, come).
At the end of a word almost always a short *a* — and it marks a **feminine** word.

blocks.title: The sound ə, and why it is never written
items: The sound **ə** (like *a* in *about*) is everywhere in Pashto — yet it is almost never written. زما (*zmā*, "my") looks vowelless; what is actually said is *zə-mā*.

This is just like Arabic, which does not write its short vowels, and it works the same way: a reader who knows the word knows its vowels. The pronunciation column in this course writes them for you until you no longer need it.
There is an official mark for it — زواکی (a small ٭ under the letter) — but Afghan books and newspapers almost never use it. Don't wait for it to appear.

blocks.text: A three-minute drill before unit 1

items: Say **ta – ṭa – ta – ṭa** ten times. For the first, the tip of the tongue touches the teeth; for the second, it curls back to touch the roof of the mouth. Feel the difference, don't just listen for it.
Say **tso** (څو) and **dzəm** (ځم) five times. These are among the few truly new sounds for an English speaker at the start of a word, and both appear in unit 1.
Read aloud: ښه · ډوډۍ · ورور · مڼه · ټول · ژبه. These six words contain all the new letters at once.

⚠️ Different — note the ې at the end.

blocks.text: 2. "To be" — present and past
3. Present-tense verb endings
4. Noun gender

blocks.title: A quick rule that covers 80% of cases
items: Ending in **ه** → feminine; the plural changes it to **ې**: ښځه → ښځې.
Ending in a consonant → masculine; the plural adds **ونه**: کور → کورونه.
Ending in **ی** *-ay* → masculine; the plural changes it to **ي** *-ī*: سړی → سړي (spelled differently, said differently, plural in meaning).
Ending in **ۍ** *-əy* → feminine, and **the plural does not change**: ډوډۍ stays ډوډۍ.
⚠️ Some words break all of these, and the most common ones do: **مور** (mother) and **خور** (sister) do not end in ه but are still feminine.

blocks.text: 5. Prepositions come in pairs

head: Pair
Meaning
Example
rows: په کابل کې *pə kābəl ke* — in Kabul
له کوره څخه *lə kora tsəkha* — from home
د ملګري سره *də malgarī sara* — with a friend
تر سبا پورې *tər sabā pore* — until tomorrow
پر مېز باندې *pər mez bānde* — on the table

blocks.text: 6. Possession: د + owner, then the thing

items: The possessive form: **د بودي کتاب** *də Būdī kitāb* — "Budi's book". Literally "of Budi book". The owner comes **first**, just like English *Budi's book*.
Pronouns have their own short forms: **زما** (my) · **ستا** (your, informal) · **د هغه** (his) · **د هغې** (her) · **زمونږ** (our) · **ستاسو** (your, pl./polite) · **د هغوی** (their).
⚠️ Remember that زما is not "I" but "my", and it cannot stand as the subject of a sentence.

blocks.text: 7. The past tense — and the rule that turns everything around

blocks.title: 🔴 The single most important rule in this whole course
items: Verbs **without an object** (go, come, sit, sleep): the subject is in the direct form, and the verb agrees with the **subject**. زه ولاړم *zə wlāṛəm* — I went. هغه ولاړه *hagha wlāṛa* — she went.

Verbs **with an object** (read, eat, see, write) in the **past**: the subject goes into the **oblique form**, and the verb agrees with the **OBJECT**. ما کتاب ولوست *mā kitāb wālost* — I read the book.
If the object is feminine, the verb changes: ما ډوډۍ وخوړه *mā ḍoḍəy wakhoṛa* — "I ate the bread", and the form وخوړه is decided by **ډوډۍ**.
If the object is plural: ما کتابونه ولوستل *mā kitābūna wālostəl*.
This rule applies **only in the past**. In the present everything is normal: زه کتاب لولم *zə kitāb lwaləm*.

blocks.text: 8. Aspect: the و- that changes the meaning completely

items: The prefix **و-** goes in front of the verb to mark a **completed** action. It is required in commands (ولیکه! write!), in a definite future, and in completed past sentences.
⚠️ When و- is added, **the stress moves onto و-**: *wə́likəl*. That stress is what really tells the meanings apart to an Afghan ear.
Verbs that already have a prefix of their own do not take و-: راتلل (to come) → **راغلم**, not **وراغلم**.

blocks.text: 9. Negation

items: The word **نه** *nə* goes **right before the verb**: زه نه ځم *zə nə dzəm* — I am not going.
Prohibitions use **مه** *ma*, not نه. For example مه ځه! *ma dza* — don't go!
"There isn't / there is no" for things: نشته *nishta*. په کور کې څوک نشته — there is nobody at home.
⚠️ Answering "yes" to a negative question means **agreeing with the negative** ("Aren't you going?" — "Yes" = "No, I'm not") — the opposite of English.

blocks.text: 10. Question words

back.title: Numbers 1–100 and how to use them

blocks.text: Pashto numbers are tidy up to twenty, and then use one habit that turns English thinking around: **the units come first, then the tens**.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Units first, tens second
items: 21 is not "twenty-one" but **یوویشت** *yaw-wisht* — literally "one-twenty". Just like German and Dutch, the reverse of English.

For example: 22 **دوه ویشت** *dwa-wisht* · 25 **پنځه ویشت** *pindzə-wisht* · 31 **یو دېرش** *yaw-dersh* · 45 **پنځه څلوېښت** *pindzə-tsalweṣt* · 68 **اته شپېته** *atə-shpeta* · 99 **نهه نوي** *nəhə-nawī*.
⚠️ Note that 20 on its own is **شل** *shəl*, but as soon as a unit stands in front of it, it becomes **ویشت** *wisht*. This is the only form that changes shape.
Numbers above a hundred are joined with **او** (and): 105 = **سل او پنځه**, 250 = **دوه سوه او پنځوس**.

blocks.text: Nouns after numbers stay singular — with one twist

items: For example **دوه کتابه** *dwa kitāba* — "two books". The noun does not take its full plural; it uses a special **counting form** (کتاب becomes کتابه).
For most masculine words, that counting form just adds **ـه**: سړی → **دوه سړي**, کور → **درې کوره**, روپۍ → **پنځه روپۍ**.
For feminine words ending in ه, the counting form is the same as the plural: ښځه → **درې ښځې**.
If you forget, using the plain singular is still understood. It is not a mistake that changes the meaning.

blocks.text: Order, money, and time

Pashto verbs are listed in their base form, which always ends in **ـل** *-əl*. The third column gives you the present-tense "I" form — the form you actually use when speaking, and some of them cannot be guessed from the base form.

blocks.title: The pattern that gives you half this list for free
items: The verb **کول** (*kawəl*, to do) attaches to a noun and instantly makes a new verb: کار **کول** (to work) · مرسته **کول** (to help) · خبرې **کول** (to talk) · انتظار **کول** (to wait). Hundreds of Pashto verbs are built this way, and only the کول part changes.

Its passive partner is **کېدل** (*kedəl*, to become): پیل **کول** = to begin (something) · پیل **کېدل** = to be begun, to start. Likewise ښه **کول** = to fix, improve · ښه **کېدل** = to get better, recover.

⚠️ Verbs ending in **ـېدل** almost always mean something **happens to** the subject (پوهېدل · رسېدل · ګرځېدل), while those ending in **ـول** mean the subject **does it to something else** (پوهول = to make understand · ګرځول = to turn something). One letter reverses the direction.

blocks.text: If you have reached this page after working through twenty units in order, you have something few learners have: the ability to open your mouth in Pashto. What follows decides whether that ability lasts.
The next four weeks

items: **Week 1 — repeat, don't add.** Go back to unit 1 and reread every dialogue aloud, one unit a day. This time cover the pronunciation column. You will be surprised how much you can already read straight from the script.
**Week 2 — write by hand.** Copy ten dialogues by hand, in joined script. Pashto script only truly becomes yours through your hand, not your eyes.

**Week 3 — listen.** Find Pashto news broadcasts (RTA Pashto, Azadi Radio, BBC Pashto) and listen fifteen minutes a day without trying to understand everything. You have one job: catch the words you already know.
**Week 4 — write five sentences a day** about your day, in the past tense. That is where the rule from unit 13 stops being theory.

Needs the ergative rule from unit 13 to be automatic first.
Needs the subjunctive forms that are fully covered in A2.
At A1 the active form is enough; the passive is rare in conversation.
High honorifics and formal letter language
Used in offices and writing, not on the street.
A2 splits it by field, once the sentence framework is solid.
The language's greatest gift — but it demands twice the vocabulary.

blocks.title: Three things Afghans will notice right away
items: **You use تاسو with people you have just met.** This, not your vocabulary, is what makes your Pashto sound grown-up.
**You put the verb at the end without thinking.** As long as you still have to think about it, your sentences will sound like a translation.
**You don't run away from ښ and ږ.** Choose one pronunciation — Kabul or Kandahar — and stick to it. What sounds odd is not the choice but switching in the middle of a sentence.

blocks.text: And one last thing that is not on any page before this one: **مېلمستیا** *melmastyā*, hospitality to guests, is not just a polite custom in Afghanistan — it is part of the code of life called پښتونولي. If you try to speak Pashto, however clumsily, you will be treated as a guest. This course cannot teach that; it can only make sure you have the words to respond.
And to close: **په مخه مو ښه!** *pə makha mo ṣa* — may the road ahead of you be good.
